I am 54 years old and have been farming my land in Quzhou for more than 30 years. I only went to primary school, so I do not read many books about farming — everything I know comes from my own experience and from watching what my neighbors do. I have about 5.7 mu of land, which is about average for a smallholder in my village.

This year I will grow the same crops I always grow: winter wheat and summer maize in rotation. I will not try anything new like cotton or vegetables because the market for those is uncertain and I cannot afford a bad year. Wheat gives my family flour to eat, and maize gives us cash income. That combination has kept us fed for decades, so I stick with it.

For the wheat, I will rotary till the soil in early October and sow an improved wheat variety — the same kind my neighbor Zhang used last year, which yielded well. I will put down about 50 kg of compound fertilizer per mu as a basal dose and topdress with urea in the spring if the wheat looks yellow. I will irrigate three times: at sowing, at jointing, and at grain filling. The electricity for pumping water is expensive, but without irrigation the yield drops too much, so I pay it. I will also spray pesticides three times — for weeds, insects, and to prevent disease.

For the maize, there is no time to till after the wheat harvest — the window is only about one week. So I will plant no-till using a hybrid variety like Nongda 372. I will apply compound fertilizer at planting, about 40–50 kg per mu, and irrigate twice. If the summer rains are good, two times is enough. I will spray for weeds and insects two or three times as needed.

I expect about 450 kg per mu of wheat and 500 kg per mu of maize. That is not the highest yield in the village, but it is steady and safe, and that is what matters for my family.
